methods.label: Separate the three possible side relationships
methods.explanation:
Use the usual interpretation that each point is chosen uniformly along the square's perimeter, independently of the other point. Each side then has probability \(1/4\); vertices have probability zero. Relative to the first point's side, the second point lies on the same side, an adjacent side, or the opposite side with probabilities \(1/4,1/2,1/4\), respectively. These three cases cover all possibilities without overlap except at vertices.

For points on the same side, let \(u,v\in[0,1]\) be their distances from one endpoint. Independence makes \((u,v)\) uniform in the unit square. The distance is \(|u-v|\), so the favorable region \(|u-v|\ge1/2\) consists of two right triangles, each with legs \(1/2\). Its total area, and hence the probability within this case, is
\[
2\left(\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12\right)=\frac14.
\]

For points on adjacent sides, let \(u,v\in[0,1]\) be their distances from the shared corner. Their distance is \(\sqrt{u^2+v^2}\). The distance is less than \(1/2\) precisely in a quarter disk of radius \(1/2\) in the unit parameter square. Its area is
\[
\frac14\pi\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac{\pi}{16}.
\]
Thus the probability of distance at least \(1/2\) within this case is \(1-\pi/16\).

For points on opposite sides, the distance is at least \(1\), so every pair succeeds. Weighting the three cases gives
\[
P=\frac14\cdot\frac14
+\frac12\left(1-\frac{\pi}{16}\right)
+\frac14
=\frac{26-\pi}{32}.
\]
The equality-distance boundaries have area zero, so their inclusion does not change these probabilities. Since \(\gcd(26,1,32)=1\), the required sum is \(26+1+32=\boxed{59}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
